question: Watch the clip below. This 1990 recording is essentially one unbroken close-up of the singer's face, and it turned a song that had quietly flopped on a 1985 album by a little-known funk side project into a worldwide number one. The singer did not write it — the man who did had handed it to a band he had assembled himself, and he only performed it live much later. Who wrote the song?

options.info: He wrote it in 1984 and gave it to The Family, a band on his own Paisley Park label. Their version sank; this cover made it a standard, and Prince only began performing it himself years afterwards.
A hugely successful voice of the same era, but he had nothing to do with this song.
He worked with the same producer circles in the late 1980s, and the guess is understandable, but the song is not his.
An Irish songwriter like the performer here, which makes him a tempting answer, but the credit belongs elsewhere.

audio.credit: Sinéad O'Connor – 'Nothing Compares 2 U' official video, via SineadOConnorVEVO on YouTube

question: Watch the clip below. The whole thing was shot guerrilla-style outside a shopping-mall cinema in Westwood, California, with a real audience that had no idea a video was being made — security tried to shut it down mid-shoot. The director appears on camera himself, in a headband, leading a deliberately terrible dance troupe, and he went on to direct feature films including 'Being John Malkovich' and 'Her'. Who directed it?

options.info: He both directed and starred as 'Richard Koufey', leader of the fictional Torrance Community Dance Group. The video won Video of the Year at the 1999 MTV VMAs, where he restaged the routine live.
The other great music-video auteur of the era, famous for handmade in-camera trickery rather than hidden-camera pranks.
Known for far darker, more grotesque clips built around prosthetics and digital horror.
Directed several landmark videos of the same years before moving to features like 'Sexy Beast' and 'Under the Skin'.

audio.credit: Fatboy Slim – 'Praise You' official video, via Fatboy Slim on YouTube

question: Watch the clip below. Shot in crisp black and white in 1990, it restages Hollywood glamour portraiture of the 1930s, with poses lifted from photographs of stars like Marlene Dietrich and Jean Harlow. Its director had just come from a run of commercials and videos and would go on to make 'Seven', 'Fight Club' and 'The Social Network'. Who directed it?

options.info: He directed several of the singer's videos around this period, and the meticulous monochrome lighting here is an early sign of the control-freak visual style his features became known for.
A fashion photographer who did direct black-and-white videos in exactly this register, which makes him the strongest decoy — but not this one.
A French photographer-director who worked with the same artist on other clips, though not this one.
Directed a string of the singer's earlier 1980s videos, but had moved on to features by 1990.

audio.credit: Madonna – 'Vogue' official video, via Madonna on YouTube

question: Watch the clip below. This 1990 hit was the first rap single to reach the top of the American album charts, and the parachute trousers in it became a fashion punchline for a decade. Its entire groove, though, is lifted wholesale from a 1981 funk record — the original artist was not credited at first, sued, and ended up with a co-writing credit and a Grammy. Which record was sampled?

options.info: The bassline is taken almost note for note. James sued, won a settlement and a songwriting credit, and shared the 1991 Grammy for Best R&B Song as a result.
The most-sampled bassline in hip hop history, underpinning 'Rapper's Delight' among many others — but not this track.
A cornerstone of P-Funk and a favourite sample source, though the groove here comes from elsewhere.

options.text: The Gap Band – 'Oops Up Side Your Head'
options.info: An early-80s funk staple with a similarly springy bass feel, which is why it works as a decoy.

audio.credit: M.C. Hammer – 'U Can't Touch This' official video, via MCHammerVevo on YouTube

question: Watch the clip below. Released in 1990, this was the first hip hop single to top the American singles chart. The rapper initially insisted his hook was original, claiming he had added an extra note — a defence nobody believed. The bassline in fact comes from a 1981 collaboration between a British rock band and a solo star, and after legal pressure both of them were added to the writing credits. Which song was it taken from?

options.text: 'Under Pressure' by Queen and David Bowie
options.info: The famous bass figure was played by John Deacon. Neither party was credited on release; a settlement followed and Queen and Bowie now appear as co-writers.

options.text: 'Another One Bites the Dust' by Queen
options.info: Also a Deacon bassline and also endlessly sampled, which makes it the most plausible wrong answer here.
A 1983 Bowie hit produced by Nile Rodgers, but its groove is nothing like the one used here.
Another instantly recognisable bass hook of the era, though unrelated to this record.

audio.credit: Vanilla Ice – 'Ice Ice Baby' official video, via vanillaiceVEVO on YouTube

question: Watch the clip below. This 1985 video is one of the most-quoted pieces of surrealism MTV ever aired: the singer sits as a top-hatted host at an absurd tea party, a caterpillar smokes a hookah, and the whole thing ends with a giant cake being sliced up. It is a direct restaging of a Victorian children's book. Which book?

options.text: 'Alice's Adventures in Wonderland' by Lewis Carroll
options.info: The singer plays the Mad Hatter, and the tea party, the caterpillar and the shrinking-and-growing gags all come straight from Carroll. The cake-cutting finale drew complaints for being disturbing.

options.text: 'The Wizard of Oz' by L. Frank Baum
options.info: American rather than Victorian British, and its imagery — yellow brick road, ruby slippers — appears nowhere in the clip.
Edwardian rather than Victorian, and there are no pirates or flying children here.
A genuine Victorian children's fantasy, which makes it a fair guess, but not the source being parodied.

audio.credit: Tom Petty and the Heartbreakers – 'Don't Come Around Here No More' official video, via TomPettyVEVO on YouTube

question: Watch the clip below. It became the most-played video in MTV's history and swept the 1987 video awards. The singer had to lie under a sheet of glass for a full day while objects — fruit, trains, dancing chickens, clay heads — crawled across his face. Almost nothing here is a normal camera take. Which technique was used to build it?

options.text: Stop-motion animation, shot one frame at a time
options.info: Animators including the Brothers Quay and the team that later made 'Wallace and Gromit' worked on it. Roughly sixteen hours of shooting produced about four minutes of finished film, with the singer holding still frame by frame.
Tracing animation onto filmed frames — the method behind 'A-ha's pencil-sketch look — but not what happens here.
CGI existed in 1986 but was crude, expensive and looked nothing like the tactile, handmade texture on screen.

options.text: Bluescreen compositing of separately filmed layers
options.info: A standard 1980s video trick, and used incidentally here, but it is not the technique the clip is famous for.

audio.credit: Peter Gabriel – 'Sledgehammer' official video, via Peter Gabriel on YouTube

question: Watch the clip below. For this 1994 video the band was digitally dropped into archive footage of a 1970s American sitcom, performing on the stage of the malt shop where its characters hung out. The show's actual cast members appear around them, and the studio had to clear the rights to insert the band into a two-decade-old episode. Which sitcom is it?

options.info: The footage comes from an episode set in Arnold's diner, and the video is introduced by Al Molaro. Henry Winkler's Fonzie even gets a dance break.
A spin-off from the correct show, set in the same era and city, which is exactly why it is the trickiest wrong answer.
'Grease' was a film, not a sitcom, though its 1950s nostalgia is close in spirit.
A 1970s American sitcom, but a suburban family comedy with no diner and no house band.

audio.credit: Weezer – 'Buddy Holly' official video, via WeezerVEVO on YouTube

question: Watch the clip below. The eleven-minute 1991 version opens with a comic prologue before the song even starts: a boy, annoyed at his father, drags a colossal stack of speakers into the living room, puts on his guitar and blasts the old man clean through the roof. That boy was, at the time, the biggest child star in the world, fresh off a Christmas blockbuster. Who is he?

options.info: He had just made 'Home Alone' and was a close friend of the singer. George Wendt of 'Cheers' plays the father who gets launched into the sky.
A famous American child actor of exactly the same years, from 'The Wonder Years', which makes him the obvious decoy.
He was a child actor in the early 1990s and did appear in other music videos of the decade, but not this one.
A teen star of 1990s American television, but slightly later and not involved here.

audio.credit: Michael Jackson – 'Black or White' official video, via michaeljacksonVEVO on YouTube

question: Watch the clip below. This 1981 synth-pop version defined the sound of the early 1980s, but the song was already fifteen years old. It was first cut in 1964 as a B-side by an American soul singer who got nowhere with it — though the record later became a cult favourite on Britain's northern soul dance floors, which is how the duo found it. The same singer later spent years as the partner of Marc Bolan of T. Rex. Who recorded the original?

options.info: Her 1964 recording flopped on release, then became a northern soul classic. She was Marc Bolan's partner and was driving the car in the 1977 crash that killed him.
An American soul singer of the same generation, best known for 'Just One Look', but not connected to this song.
The similar first name makes her a natural trap, but her fame came a decade later with disco.
A pioneering rhythm-and-blues singer, though her peak came in the 1950s and this is not one of hers.

audio.credit: Soft Cell – 'Tainted Love' official video, via SoftCellVEVO on YouTube

question: Watch the clip below. Its central effect — the singer apparently gliding, sliding and moonwalking across a floor that carries him wherever he goes — won Video of the Year in 1997 and was widely assumed to involve either a treadmill or computer trickery. It is in fact an entirely practical, in-camera illusion. How was it actually done?

options.text: The floor stayed still and the walls and furniture were moved around it
options.info: The set was built so that the walls, skirting boards and sofa slid on hidden rails while the camera moved with them. The dancer simply walked normally; everything else did the travelling.

options.text: The singer danced on a concealed treadmill built into the floor
options.info: The most common guess, but a treadmill would not explain the sideways and diagonal glides.

options.text: The whole room was computer-generated around a bluescreen performance
options.info: 1996 CGI could not have produced this crisp a result on a music-video budget, and the shadows are real.

options.text: The room was built on a giant rotating turntable
options.info: Rotating sets are a real film technique, famously used in '2001: A Space Odyssey', but the motion here is linear, not circular.

audio.credit: Jamiroquai – 'Virtual Insanity' official video, via JamiroquaiVEVO on YouTube

question: Watch the clip below. Released in 1998, the video is a single unsettling image: a computer-generated foetus in the womb, mouthing the words. The song's harpsichord-and-heartbeat opening later became one of the most recognisable television theme tunes of the 2000s, played over the title card of an American medical drama about a misanthropic diagnostician. Which series used it?

options.info: The instrumental opening ran under the titles from 2004 onwards, so closely identified with the show that many viewers assumed it had been written for it.
A contemporary American medical drama, but its theme was a different song entirely.
The dominant hospital drama of the 1990s, but it used a purpose-composed orchestral theme.
Another moody premium-cable series of the 2000s with a famous theme, though a different one.

audio.credit: Massive Attack – 'Teardrop' official video, via MassiveAttackVEVO on YouTube

question: Watch the clip below. The song came out in 1979, and the video — all plastic tubes, a woman in a glass cylinder and a very knowing bit of retro-futurism — is remembered less for itself than for the slot it occupied. At one minute past midnight on 1 August 1981, it was the very first thing broadcast on a brand-new American cable channel. Which channel launched with it?

options.info: The channel signed on with this clip, an unusually apt choice given the title. The second video played was Pat Benatar's 'You Better Run'.
A sister music channel, but it did not launch until 1985, aimed at an older audience.
A cable channel that started in 1972 with films and sport, not music videos.
Launched in 1980, a year earlier, and as a news network it never played music videos.

audio.credit: The Buggles – 'Video Killed the Radio Star' official video, via TheBugglesVEVO on YouTube

question: Watch the clip below. This thunderous 2015 version, all candlelight and close-ups, was so far removed from the whispered folk original that the band who wrote the song personally sent the singer a note of approval after seeing it. The original was recorded half a century earlier by an American duo whose acoustic take was famously remixed with drums and electric guitar without their knowledge, turning it into a number-one hit. Which act recorded the original version of this song?

options.info: Paul Simon and Art Garfunkel first released the song in 1964; a producer later overdubbed electric instruments without telling them, and the rebuilt version topped the US charts in 1966.
The close-harmony duo were a huge influence on Simon & Garfunkel, but this song was never theirs.
The folk trio shared the same Greenwich Village scene and covered plenty of contemporaries, but not this song in its original release.
The Byrds specialised in electrifying folk material, most famously Dylan's, which makes them a plausible guess here, but wrong.

audio.credit: Disturbed – 'The Sound Of Silence' official video, via Disturbed on YouTube

question: Watch the clip below. This 2006 single was the singer's first US number one, and the reason it sounds instantly familiar is that its entire backing track is built on the pounding synth riff of an early-1980s British synth-pop smash — itself a cover of an obscure 1960s northern-soul record. Which song is being sampled?

options.info: Soft Cell's 1981 version of Gloria Jones' 1964 soul obscurity became a global hit; its bare two-note synth hook is looped underneath this track from start to finish.
New Order's 1983 classic is one of the most-sampled dance records ever, but it is not the source here.

options.text: 'Just Can't Get Enough' by Depeche Mode
options.info: Depeche Mode's 1981 debut-era hit shares the same era and the same bouncy synth palette, which makes it a tempting decoy.

options.text: 'Don't You Want Me' by The Human League
options.info: Another 1981 synth-pop landmark, but its sample history runs elsewhere.

audio.credit: Rihanna – 'SOS' official music video, via RihannaVEVO on YouTube

question: Watch the clip below. Shot in 2001 in the deserted lobby and atrium of a Los Angeles hotel, this video consists almost entirely of one middle-aged Hollywood actor dancing — leaping off banisters, sliding across marble and eventually flying — in a business suit. He had trained as a dancer as a teenager long before he became a star of unsettling character roles, and the video swept the MTV awards that year. Who is the dancing actor?

options.info: Walken began as a musical-theatre dancer in his teens and had been waiting decades for a role that used it; his solo here won the clip six MTV Video Music Awards.
Goldblum has the eccentric physicality for it and has done his share of odd cameos, but this is not him.
Murray is a famous scene-stealer in unexpected music-video and indie appearances, which makes him a reasonable guess.
Malkovich has appeared in famously surreal screen projects, but he does not appear in this video.

audio.credit: Fatboy Slim ft. Bootsy Collins – 'Weapon Of Choice' official video, via Fatboy Slim on YouTube

question: Watch the clip below. Filmed in 2015 in the Beaugrenelle district of Paris, it follows a squad of women marching and drilling through concrete plazas while the camera warps, splits and mirrors the tower blocks around them. The handmade, in-camera trickery is the signature of a French director better known for a certain 2004 film about erased memories, and for a career of famously homemade-looking videos. Who directed it?

options.info: Gondry made his name on optical illusions built in-camera rather than in post, and later directed 'Eternal Sunshine of the Spotless Mind'.
Jonze shares the same generation of video auteurs and the same absurdist streak, but this one isn't his.
Cunningham is the go-to name for nightmarish electronic-music visuals, which makes him a plausible fit for a dance record.
Glazer moved from landmark videos and adverts into features, but he did not direct this clip.

audio.credit: The Chemical Brothers ft. Q-Tip – 'Go' official music video, via ChemicalBrothersVEVO on YouTube

question: Watch the clip below. Three dancers, one black-and-white studio, no cuts to speak of — the routine in this 2008 video became a worldwide craze, but it was openly lifted from a 1969 television dance number performed on The Ed Sullivan Show. The choreographer of that original was a Broadway and film director famous for hunched shoulders, turned-in knees and bowler hats. Whose choreography is being reworked?

options.info: The routine reworks Fosse's 'Mexican Breakfast', danced on television in 1969 by Gwen Verdon; the singer has said she watched the clip and built the video around it.
Berkeley's kaleidoscopic overhead formations defined the 1930s movie musical, but his style is mass geometry rather than this angular trio work.
Graham revolutionised modern concert dance, a very different lineage from Broadway jazz.
Cunningham's chance-based avant-garde choreography has little to do with this routine.

audio.credit: Beyoncé – 'Single Ladies (Put a Ring on It)' official video, via BeyoncéVEVO on YouTube

question: Watch the clip below. This 2017 video is a rapid-fire chain of staged tableaux, and one of the most-discussed shots restages a famous Renaissance mural: the rapper sits at the centre of a long table with figures clustered on either side of him. Which artwork is being recreated?

options.info: The shot mirrors Leonardo's late-15th-century mural in Milan, with the rapper in the central Christ position and the surrounding figures grouped in threes.
The Sistine Chapel ceiling panel of two nearly touching hands is often parodied in videos, but that is not the composition here.
Rembrandt's crowded militia group portrait is a favourite for restagings, though its diagonal chaos looks nothing like this symmetrical table.
Botticelli's Venus on a shell is a pop-culture staple, but it appears nowhere in this clip.

audio.credit: Kendrick Lamar – 'HUMBLE.' official video, via KendrickLamarVEVO on YouTube

question: Watch the clip below. Shot in 2007 by director Hype Williams, this video is a near shot-for-shot tribute to a landmark 1988 Japanese animated film: the neon-lit medical laboratory, the figure strapped to a gurney, the pale test subjects and the motorbike are all drawn from it. Which film is being homaged?

options.info: Katsuhiro Otomo's 1988 cyberpunk classic set in Neo-Tokyo supplies the lab, the gurney, the wrinkled child-like subjects and the famous bike.
Mamoru Oshii's 1995 film is the other great cyberpunk anime touchstone, but it came out seven years later and isn't the source here.
Ridley Scott's 1982 film shaped the whole rain-and-neon look these videos borrow, though it is live action and not the direct reference.
Shinya Tsukamoto's 1989 body-horror cult film shares the industrial nightmare mood but not the imagery used here.

audio.credit: Kanye West – 'Stronger' official video, via KanyeWestVEVO on YouTube

question: Watch the clip below. Released in 2018 and dissected frame by frame for months afterwards, this video keeps the singer dancing in the foreground while chaos unfolds behind him in long, gliding takes inside a warehouse. It was made by the same director who shot much of the surreal TV series 'Atlanta' with the same performer. Who directed it?

options.info: Murai is the long-time visual collaborator behind 'Atlanta' and this clip, known for deadpan framing that lets disaster happen quietly in the background.
DuVernay has directed both documentary and blockbuster features and occasional music videos, but not this one.
Matsoukas is one of the era's most acclaimed video directors and moved into features too, which makes her a strong decoy.
Jenkins is a celebrated feature director with a very different, more lyrical camera style; he did not direct this.

audio.credit: Childish Gambino – 'This Is America' official video, via ChildishGambinoVEVO on YouTube

question: Watch the clip below. In this 2002 video the singer walks along a wooded path and through a wrecked car scene while everything around him — falling leaves, rain, glass — behaves impossibly. The whole thing was filmed and then played back the other way round, which meant the singer had to spend weeks preparing for one specific technical demand before shooting. What did he have to learn?

options.text: To sing the entire song backwards, phonetically, so it would look right once the film was reversed
options.info: He spent roughly a month drilling the lyrics in reverse; played forwards the footage runs backwards, but his mouth appears to be singing the song normally.

options.text: To lip-sync at half speed so the footage could be sped up
options.info: Speed-ramping is a common video trick, but the illusion here depends on direction rather than tempo.

options.text: To perform the whole song in sign language
options.info: Sign-language performances have featured in other videos, but not in this one.

options.text: To sing while fully submerged in water
options.info: Underwater shoots are a real music-video staple, and this clip does involve rain, but that is not the challenge here.

audio.credit: Coldplay – 'The Scientist' official video, via Coldplay on YouTube

question: Watch the clip below. The 2006 video was shot in a single unbroken take in a garage for almost no money, won a Grammy for Best Short Form Music Video, and became one of the first videos to go viral through YouTube rather than television. The four band members spend the entire song performing a tightly choreographed routine on top of eight pieces of ordinary gym equipment. What are they dancing on?

options.info: The band rehearsed the routine for roughly a month; the video was directed by singer Damian Kulash's sister, Trish Sie.
Never used by the band, though the video's low-budget garage aesthetic has invited plenty of imitations.
Not used here — the routine depends on the performers being able to walk, run and step sideways between machines.
Wrong band and wrong video, though the group did later build routines around moving vehicles, robotic arms and zero gravity.

audio.credit: OK Go – 'Here It Goes Again' official video, via OKGoVEVO on YouTube

question: Watch the clip below. This 2005 track later turned up in a hit teen drama and was parodied to death online, but its strange choral sound has no choir, no piano and no guitar on it at all. The singer produced the record herself, and every sound you hear comes from one source processed through one particular piece of studio equipment. What is that trick?

options.text: Her own voice run through a vocal harmoniser, which builds the chords from the notes she plays on its keyboard
options.info: She used a DigiTech vocal-processing workstation: she sang into it while playing chords, and the box generated the stacked harmony parts from her single live voice.

options.text: A church pipe organ recorded in an empty cathedral
options.info: The sustained, breathy chords do resemble an organ, which is exactly why the effect fools people, but no organ was used.

options.text: Auto-Tune applied to a heavily distorted piano
options.info: Auto-Tune corrects or warps pitch on an existing signal; it does not create the multi-part harmony heard here.

options.text: A theremin doubled by a string section
options.info: The theremin produces a single wavering tone, nothing like the blocky chordal texture of this recording.

audio.credit: Imogen Heap – 'Hide And Seek' official video, via ImogenHeapVEVO on YouTube

question: Watch the clip below. A comic Korean singer, a horse-riding dance and a parody of a wealthy Seoul district turned this 2012 clip into a global phenomenon, and in December of that year it set a record that no video had ever reached before. What was that milestone?

options.text: It became the first YouTube video ever to pass one billion views
options.info: It crossed the billion mark in December 2012 and later grew so large that YouTube had to rebuild its view counter, which had been capped at about 2.1 billion.

options.text: It became the first non-English song to top the US Billboard Hot 100
options.info: The song was enormous in the United States but stalled at number two on the Hot 100.

options.text: It became the first music video to win a Grammy
options.info: The Grammys have had a music-video category since the 1980s, so this would not have been a first.

options.text: It became the first video to reach one billion likes
options.info: No video has come close to a billion likes; the record in question was about views.

audio.credit: PSY – 'Gangnam Style' official video, via officialpsy on YouTube
